docs.title: Provider Datalab
docs.text:
Provider Datalab creates shared data workspaces on Kubernetes. Teams declare users, sessions, and managed services in a Datalab resource. Crossplane creates the resources from the platform's EnvironmentConfig.

Sessions provide editors, terminals, and persistent workspaces. The shared Data service, packageR, provides object-storage browsing and file sharing. Datalabs can also request PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Redis.

Task Guide Prepare the platform Installation and EnvironmentConfig reference Manage sessions, stores, and shared files Use a Datalab Protect browser and machine access Authentication Read data with AWS tools S3 client access Run Dask, MLflow, or psql Additional services Review access controls Security Look up Datalab fields API reference

ADR-001 records why Datalab is the public API and runtime resources stay internal. ADR-002 records why PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Redis are managed services and how users and the platform operator share responsibility.

docs.title: ADR-001: Use Datalab as the Public Contract
Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
Implemented.

Users create a Datalab. Provider Datalab turns it into a working data workspace and reports session information on the same resource.

Educates is the first implementation of runtime sessions. It provides the browser editor and terminal. Its resources are created and managed internally.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
A data workspace needs many things: an editor, a terminal, persistent files, credentials, networking, and optional services. Exposing every resource needed to build that workspace would give users a complicated and fragile API.

We need one stable contract that describes what a user wants, while allowing the implementation behind it to change.

docs.title: Make Datalab the only public workspace resource
docs.text:
Users and GitOps tools work with the namespaced Datalab resource. It describes the desired workspace, including its named sessions and optional capabilities.

The Datalab name, namespace, and UID form its stable identity. Generated Pod, Secret, and runtime-resource names are not part of the public contract.

docs.title: Keep the runtime implementation internal
docs.text:
The internal runtime provides the editor, terminal, workspace Pod, sessions, and optional applications. Crossplane translates a Datalab into the runtime and Kubernetes resources required to run it.

This translation is an implementation detail:

User or GitOps tool
  -> Datalab
     -> Provider Datalab reconciliation
        -> internal runtime resources
           -> working Datalab session

Clients never create, update, discover, or depend on runtime resources directly. Crossplane owns those generated resources. This keeps one source of truth and lets the runtime implementation evolve without changing how users manage a Datalab.

The same rule applies if the internal runtime changes later. Runtime resources remain projections of the Datalab and do not become a second public workspace API.

docs.title: Keep user choices separate from operator policy
docs.text:
The Datalab spec contains choices that a user is allowed to make. The operator-owned EnvironmentConfig contains platform settings such as ingress, Keycloak realm, storage classes, security defaults, and extension packages.

Crossplane combines both sets of input. Users therefore get a small API, while operators keep control of security and infrastructure policy.

docs.title: Manage sessions through the Datalab
docs.text:
Each session has a unique name and a desired state such as started or stopped. Provider Datalab creates the internal runtime for started sessions and reports the observed phase, message, and browser URL in Datalab.status.sessions. A stopped session keeps its workspace PVC.

Clients read the Datalab status. They do not look up the internal runtime. Diagnostic phase and message text is not a stable machine-readable lifecycle API; richer clients will need typed status fields.

The current API does not have a separate environment or profile object. Add such concepts only through a separate decision and a compatible API change.

docs.title: Keep credentials out of the API
docs.text:
Credentials are read from referenced Kubernetes Secrets and copied only where the runtime needs them. Secret values never belong in the Datalab spec, status, logs, or normal client output.

Credentials and security settings currently apply to the whole Datalab. Use separate Datalabs when workloads need separate Kubernetes control planes or a stronger trust boundary.

docs.title: Add tools without changing the contract
docs.text: Operators can add runtime tools through extension packages. This keeps the Datalab API stable and avoids putting every tool in one large base image.

docs.title: Why This Design
docs.text: Design choice Reason One Datalab API Users have one clear object to create, review, and manage. Runtime stays internal Clients are not coupled to runtime-specific resources or names. Crossplane owns generated resources Reconciliation has one owner and does not compete with user changes. User input and operator policy are separate Self-service does not bypass platform security or infrastructure rules. Status is copied to the Datalab Clients do not need broad access to internal resources. Credentials stay in Secrets The public API does not become a credential-delivery channel.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Provider Datalab is self-contained: clients need only the Datalab API.
  • Changing the internal runtime does not require a second public workspace model.
  • Crossplane remains responsible for generated-resource ownership and cleanup.
  • Operators must validate user-selectable Secret references and other policy-sensitive options.
  • Render tests check generated resources; live tests must also check session transitions and access to services.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Teams need relational databases, document databases, and key-value stores for their applications and data work. They need to request these capabilities without deploying database servers or maintaining backup jobs themselves.

The platform operator needs control over storage, access, maintenance, and recovery. A common service API lets users work independently within those controls and lets the operator provide defined service guarantees.

docs.title: Offer services through Datalab
docs.text:
Use the Datalab API to request these managed services:

Capability Service Datalab field Relational database with SQL and transactions PostgreSQL spec.databases Document database MongoDB spec.documentStores Key-value store and cache Redis spec.cacheStores

Crossplane creates the service resources. The installed database operators manage their workloads. Services belong to the Datalab and continue to run when an interactive session stops. Connection settings are supplied through the Datalab connection Secret.

docs.title: Keep user configuration small
docs.text:
Users select a service, name it, and set its data storage size. For PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Redis, they can also set backupStorage to enable backups and size a separate backup volume:

spec:
  databases:
    pg0:
      names:
      - app
      storage: 10Gi
      backupStorage: 30Gi
  documentStores:
    documents:
      storage: 10Gi
      backupStorage: 30Gi
  cacheStores:
    cache:
      storage: 1Gi
      backupStorage: 3Gi

A positive backupStorage enables PostgreSQL, MongoDB, or Redis backups. Zero or an omitted value disables them. PostgreSQL uses pgBackRest; MongoDB uses a composition-managed dump job. Redis uses a composition-managed RDB snapshot job. A data volume alone is not a backup. The backup guide defines the current schedules, retention, and recovery limits.

Users configure the Datalab resource. Crossplane owns the generated resources and can replace manual changes during reconciliation.

docs.title: Assign service operations to the platform operator
docs.text:
Users own their application data, schemas, queries, and requested capacity. The platform operator owns service deployment, supported configurations, upgrades, storage classes, access controls, and operational support. Operator settings come from the platform's EnvironmentConfig.

For enabled backups, the operator must monitor failures and available space, test restores, and provide a recovery procedure. Users do not need to manage backup tools or database operator resources.

docs.title: Define the guarantees for each offered service
docs.text:
The operator must define the supported availability, backup retention, acceptable data loss, recovery time, and data deletion rules. These guarantees depend on the deployed service, storage, and tested recovery procedure. Setting a backup volume size alone does not establish them.

The service API provides consistent provisioning, persistent storage, and connection settings. High availability, recovery after loss of the cluster, and backup retention after Datalab deletion need separate operator provisions.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Users can request common data services and backups through one resource, without a separate database deployment or backup workflow.
  • The platform operator has clear responsibility for operations and the guarantees offered to users.
  • Service data is independent of session state. Its retention still depends on Datalab deletion and storage reclaim rules.
  • Users select from supported service settings. Other database products or configurations need a separate platform decision.

docs.title: Additional services
docs.text:
Run services such as Dask or MLflow as Kubernetes workloads from your Datalab terminal. These examples need Kubernetes API access and permission to create Pods, Deployments, Services, and PVCs in the target namespace. If the Datalab has no session, declare one first.

Use a vCluster for tools that need their own CRDs, controllers, or cluster roles. For a short-lived process, you can run it in the terminal and use the editor's Ports tab to open its web interface.

Use the Datalab service fields for managed PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Redis stores. The environment also supplies a session registry.

docs.title: Dask
docs.text:
Dask runs tasks across a scheduler and workers. This example creates one scheduler and one worker in the current namespace. Connect to the scheduler from Python with dask.distributed.Client.

kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: dask-scheduler
spec:
  selector:
    app: dask-scheduler
  ports:
    - name: tcp-scheduler
      port: 8786
      targetPort: 8786
    - name: http-dashboard
      port: 8787
      targetPort: 8787
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: dask-scheduler
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: dask-scheduler
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: dask-scheduler
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: scheduler
          image: daskdev/dask:2025.4.0
          args: ["dask-scheduler", "--dashboard-address", ":8787"]
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8786
            - containerPort: 8787
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: "500m", memory: "1Gi"}
            limits:   {cpu: "1",    memory: "2Gi"}
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: dask-worker
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: dask-worker
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: dask-worker
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: worker
          image: daskdev/dask:2025.4.0
          args: ["dask-worker", "tcp://dask-scheduler:8786", "--nthreads", "2", "--memory-limit", "2GB"]
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: "500m", memory: "1Gi"}
            limits:   {cpu: "1",    memory: "2Gi"}
EOF

Open the scheduler dashboard through the editor's Ports tab:

kubectl port-forward svc/dask-scheduler 8787:8787

Dask Gateway also needs cluster-wide resources. Use a vCluster or ask the operator to install it. With the dask Helm repository configured, run:

helm repo update
helm upgrade --install dask-gateway dask/dask-gateway \
  -n "${DEFAULT_NAMESPACE:-default}" \
  --create-namespace \
  --set gateway.auth.type=simple \
  --set gateway.auth.simple.password='' \
  --set traefik.service.type=ClusterIP \
  --set gateway.backend.image.name=ghcr.io/dask/dask-gateway \
  --set gateway.backend.image.tag=2025.4.0 \
  --wait --atomic

docs.title: MLflow
docs.text:
MLflow records experiment runs and their artifacts. This example stores its SQLite database on a PVC and artifacts in an existing S3 bucket. Set BUCKET to a bucket your Datalab can write to.

The PVC belongs to the current namespace. Check namespace deletion rules and the volume's reclaim policy before storing records you need to keep. For a shared service, use a managed database and arrange artifact backups with the operator.

export BUCKET=s-jeff # Use a bucket your Datalab can write to.

kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: minio-creds
type: Opaque
stringData:
  accessKey: "${AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID}"
  secretKey: "${AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}"
  sessionToken: "${AWS_SESSION_TOKEN:-}"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: minio-config
data:
  endpoint: "${AWS_ENDPOINT_URL}"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: mlflow
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: mlflow
spec:
  selector:
    app: mlflow
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 5000
      targetPort: 5000
      protocol: TCP
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: mlflow
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: mlflow
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: mlflow
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: mlflow
          image: ghcr.io/mlflow/mlflow:v3.14.0
          command: ["/bin/sh","-lc"]
          args:
            - |
              python -m pip install --no-cache-dir --upgrade pip &&
              pip install --no-cache-dir boto3 &&
              exec mlflow server \
                --backend-store-uri sqlite:////mlflow/mlflow.db \
                --serve-artifacts \
                --artifacts-destination s3://"${BUCKET}"/mlruns \
                --host 0.0.0.0 --port 5000 \
                --workers 2 \
                --allowed-hosts '*' \
                --cors-allowed-origins '*'
          ports:
            - containerPort: 5000
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "100m", memory: "512Mi" }
            limits:   { cpu: "300m", memory: "2Gi" }
          env:
            - name: MLFLOW_S3_ENDPOINT_URL
              valueFrom:
                configMapKeyRef: { name: minio-config, key: endpoint }
            - name: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef: { name: minio-creds, key: accessKey }
            - name: AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef: { name: minio-creds, key: secretKey }
            - name: AWS_SESSION_TOKEN
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef: { name: minio-creds, key: sessionToken }
            - name: AWS_S3_FORCE_PATH_STYLE
              value: "true"
            - name: AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED
              value: "true"
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /mlflow
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: "/", port: 5000 }
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: "/", port: 5000 }
            initialDelaySeconds: 20
            periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
        - name: data
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: mlflow
EOF

Open the MLflow interface through the editor's Ports tab:

kubectl port-forward svc/mlflow 5000:5000

Point your code at the forwarded tracking server:

export MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI="http://127.0.0.1:5000"

docs.title: PostgreSQL with psql
docs.text:
The Jeff example provides POSTGRES_PG0_DEV_URL for database dev on pg0. Run this command from a session with that variable to start a psql Pod in the current namespace:

envsubst '${POSTGRES_PG0_DEV_URL}' <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: pgsql-debug
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
  - name: psql
    image: postgres:17
    stdin: true
    tty: true
    command:
      - sh
      - -lc
      - |
        exec psql "$POSTGRES_URL"
    env:
      - name: POSTGRES_URL
        value: ${POSTGRES_PG0_DEV_URL}
EOF

Attach to the Pod after it starts:

kubectl attach -it pgsql-debug

Check the connection with a temporary table:

\set ON_ERROR_STOP on
CREATE TEMP TABLE datalab_check (value text);
INSERT INTO datalab_check VALUES ('ready');
SELECT value FROM datalab_check;

docs.title: Keep or remove a service
docs.text: Remove test services when the experiment ends. Before keeping one, agree with the platform team on its storage, backups, monitoring, upgrades, and deletion. Back up the service data separately from the session volume.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: The platform ingress controller protects Datalab sessions. Configure sign-in and authorization before users start a session. The examples below use Kyverno policies to configure NGINX or APISIX session Ingress objects.

docs.title: Keycloak clients and roles
docs.text:
Users in spec.users must already exist in the realm selected by EnvironmentConfig.data.iam.realm. Provider Datalab creates a confidential client named after the Datalab, groups for its users and administrators, and their memberships and role mappings. The client disables implicit, device, and direct access grants. Role scope mappings limit the Datalab client roles included in its tokens.

Role Assigned to Used for ws_access Datalab users Browser access ws_admin Datalab administrators Browser access with the admin role ws_api The client service account Machine access through client credentials

The runtime Secret <datalab>-oauth2-client contains client_id and client_secret. Anyone who can read it can request a machine token for that Datalab. Give access only to users and services that need it.

A service can require extra token audiences. List them in EnvironmentConfig.data.iam.extraAudiences and use the same values in the service's token checks. The S3 endpoint adds the Datalab client ID as an audience when enabled. Other OAuth clients that call these services must emit the required audience and roles too.

docs.title: Generated session resources
docs.text:
For a Datalab named s-jane with a default session, set ingress.domain to lab.acme.com. The session ingress hosts include:

s-jane-default.lab.acme.com
editor-s-jane-default.lab.acme.com
s-jane-default-editor.lab.acme.com
data-s-jane-default.lab.acme.com
s-jane-default-data.lab.acme.com

The generated ingresses carry labels that are suitable for platform policy:

training.educates.dev/application: workshop
training.educates.dev/component: session
training.educates.dev/environment.name: s-jane

For s-jane, the generated client includes redirect and web-origin entries for the Datalab root and each declared session host:

https://s-jane.lab.acme.com/*
https://s-jane-default.lab.acme.com/*
https://editor-s-jane-default.lab.acme.com/*
https://s-jane-default-editor.lab.acme.com/*
https://data-s-jane-default.lab.acme.com/*
https://s-jane-default-data.lab.acme.com/*
http://localhost:*

A service that belongs to s-jane can use this client. Shared browser ingress can use a central platform client and check the generated Datalab roles.

To call a Datalab-owned service with a machine token, read client_id and client_secret from <datalab>-oauth2-client, request a token with grant_type=client_credentials, then send that access token to the service. Its policy should require ws_api and any configured audience.

docs.title: Set the shared ingress settings
docs.text:
Set the ingress class, domain, and TLS Secret in the EnvironmentConfig. Use the same values in the session runtime installation, for example:

clusterIngressDomain: lab.acme.com
clusterIngressClass: apisix
tlsCertificateRef:
  name: wildcard-tls
  namespace: workspace

Use a wildcard certificate for *.lab.acme.com.

docs.title: Apply ingress policy
docs.text: Apply controller settings through platform policy so they cover every session Ingress. The examples use Kyverno CEL policies. They need CRDs that serve MutatingPolicy and GeneratingPolicy in policies.kyverno.io/v1. Kyverno is required for these policies, not for Provider Datalab itself. Adapt the domains, issuer, and controller settings in the linked manifests.

docs.title: NGINX Ingress with OAuth2 Proxy
docs.text:
Run OAuth2 Proxy as a shared service with its own OAuth client. Use a redirect URI such as https://auth.lab.acme.com/oauth2/callback. Its authorization policy must check access to the Datalab named in the requested host.

Apply the NGINX policy to add external-auth annotations to matching session Ingress objects. Set the proxy cookie domain to cover the session hosts, for example .lab.acme.com, and allow redirects only to that domain.

docs.title: APISIX Ingress configured by Kyverno
docs.text:
The APISIX manifest gives Kyverno permission to create ApisixPluginConfig resources, generates one in each session namespace, and attaches it to matching Ingress objects. APISIX checks incoming requests; Kyverno configures the resources.

The example uses openid-connect with a central public client named datalab-sessions. Its opa entry points to an external OPA service. The manifest does not deploy that service or supply its policy. Configure both for your platform so that the authorizer checks access to the requested Datalab. OPA is needed only for this example.

The policies do not read Secrets. For a confidential central client, use the ingress controller's supported Secret mechanism to supply its credential.

The plugin forwards the access token in Authorization and disables ID token, userinfo, and refresh token forwarding. Check that your authorizer and upstream service accept these settings.

Kyverno generates the plugin's session secret once. Synchronization is disabled to keep it stable. After changing the template, recreate an existing generated plugin config or restart its session to apply the change.

For another ingress controller, match session Ingress objects by label and domain, then attach its authentication and authorization settings.

docs.title: Install Provider Datalab
docs.text: Run these commands from a repository checkout with access to the target cluster. For a shared installation, manage manifests and Secrets through your platform's GitOps and Secret tools.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
The cluster needs Crossplane, the Educates session runtime, an ingress controller, Keycloak, and an S3-compatible object store. The CNI must enforce Kubernetes NetworkPolicy. Use Crossplane from the supported range in the package's metadata.

Install the session runtime with its CRDs and controller RBAC before creating Datalabs. Follow the runtime installation guide. The runtime ingress class, domain, and TLS Secret must match the settings below.

Install the operators for the managed stores you plan to offer. Provider Datalab integration tests use these versions:

Datalab field Operator Test version Required resource API spec.databases Crunchy PostgreSQL Operator (PGO) 6.0.2 PostgresCluster in postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/v1 spec.documentStores MongoDB Kubernetes Operator 1.14.0 MongoDBCommunity in mongodbcommunity.mongodb.com/v1 spec.cacheStores Opstree Redis Operator 0.27.0 (Helm chart 0.27.0) Redis in redis.redis.opstreelabs.in/v1beta2

These are fixed test pins. Other versions need validation before use. The harness applies each chart's CRDs before it installs or upgrades the operator.

See managed service types for the request fields and type defaults. Check the served APIs and fields before upgrading an operator. The integration tests contain the dependency settings used by this repository. Configure storage, backup and restore, monitoring, and deletion for each store you offer.

PostgreSQL without backups requires Crunchy PGO 5.7 or later. MongoDB Community backups use a composition-managed CronJob and the matching MongoDB image's database tools. Redis backups use a CronJob with the standard Redis tools image at the same Redis version as the server. Provider Kubernetes needs the batch/cronjobs permissions in dependencies/rbac.yaml. Backup volumes need a StorageClass that supports ReadWriteOnce. See backup settings for schedules, retention, and restore limits.

Gateway exposure also needs a Gateway API controller. Data uses HTTPRoute with HTTP and TLS-terminating HTTPS listeners. External PostgreSQL access uses TLSRoute in gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1 and direct TLS with SNI.

For spec.vclusters, apply the supplied provider RBAC and configure an HTTPS issuer, allowed StorageClasses, and an HTTPS Gateway listener. The host needs ValidatingAdmissionPolicy and BackendTLSPolicy support. See virtual cluster setup.

docs.title: 1. Choose the claim namespace
docs.text:
This guide uses workspace for Datalab resources and their namespaced ProviderConfigs:

kubectl create namespace workspace
kubectl create namespace datalab

Input storage Secrets live in datalab, as set by storage.secretNamespace in the environment examples. Each Datalab also has a separate namespace for its runtime and shared services.

docs.title: 2. Install provider dependencies
docs.text:
Apply the files in dependencies/ in this order:

File Purpose 00-mrap.yaml Activate the managed resource kinds used by the composition. 01-deploymentRuntimeConfigs.yaml Set provider and function Pod security. 02-providers.yaml Install the Kubernetes, Helm, and Keycloak providers. 03-providerConfigs.yaml Configure those providers in the claim namespace. functions.yaml Install the composition functions. rbac.yaml Grant provider-kubernetes access to the resources it manages.

Apply 03-providerConfigs.yaml with kubectl apply -n workspace -f .... Create its referenced Keycloak credential Secret in that namespace through your platform's Secret tools. The Keycloak account needs permission to manage clients, service-account roles, groups, memberships, and role mappings in the target realm.

Use the package pins in the dependency manifests. Wait for the provider and function revisions to report healthy before installing the configuration package. The provider-kubernetes RBAC includes access to Pods for readiness checks and PVCs for session storage.

docs.title: 3. Install the configuration package
docs.text:
Save this resource as configuration.yaml. Replace 0.12.0-rc.1 with the release tag you want to install.

apiVersion: pkg.crossplane.io/v1
kind: Configuration
metadata:
  name: datalab
spec:
  package: ghcr.io/versioneer-tech/provider-datalab:0.12.0-rc.1
  skipDependencyResolution: true

Apply it and check the package conditions:

kubectl apply -f configuration.yaml
kubectl get configurations.pkg.crossplane.io
kubectl get configurationrevisions.pkg.crossplane.io

The package installs the Datalab resource definition and composition. Its providers and functions are managed separately by the platform.

The package build reads responseTTL: 5m from composition/settings.yaml. It applies the value to every Python response and the auto-ready input. To change it, rebuild the composition and release a new package.

docs.title: 4. Set the shared environment
docs.text:
Create an EnvironmentConfig named datalab with values for your cluster. This example uses a permanent Data Ingress:

apiVersion: apiextensions.crossplane.io/v1beta1
kind: EnvironmentConfig
metadata:
  name: datalab
data:
  iam:
    realm: acme
    issuerURL: https://identity.acme.com/realms/acme
    internalURL: http://keycloak.keycloak:8080/realms/acme
  ingress:
    enabled: true
    class: nginx
    domain: lab.acme.com
    secret: wildcard-tls
    annotations: {}
  storage:
    endpoint: https://s3.acme.com
    provider: Other
    region: us-east-1
    forcePathStyle: "true"
    secretNamespace: datalab
    type: s3
  storageClasses:
    allowed:
    - sbs-default
    - sbs-default-retain
  network:
    externalEgressCIDRs:
    - 0.0.0.0/0
    - ::/0
    serviceCIDR: "10.43.0.0/16"
    podCIDRs:
    - 10.42.0.0/16
    blacklistIPs:
    - 169.254.169.254/32
    - fd00:ec2::254/128
    - 169.254.42.42/32
    - fd00:42::42/128
    excludePolicies: []
  defaults:
    vcluster:
      enabled: true
    registry:
      enabled: true
      storage: 5Gi
    data:
      enabled: true
      readOnlyMount: false
    overallQuota:
      storage: 100Gi
    security:
      externalEgress: true

Replace the example storage classes, network ranges, and DNS names before applying it. Configure authentication before users start sessions.

docs.title: Data address
docs.text:
Enable either ingress.enabled or httpRoute.enabled for a permanent Data address. Enabling both stops reconciliation. With neither enabled, Data is available through a session's authenticated ingress.

For Gateway API exposure, replace the example's ingress.enabled: true with false and add:

data:
  httpRoute:
    enabled: true
    parentName: default
    parentNamespace: contour
    sectionName: workspaces-https
    httpSectionName: workspaces-http

The Gateway needs HTTP and TLS-terminating HTTPS listeners and must accept routes from runtime namespaces. It manages the permanent Data certificate. Keep the ingress class and TLS Secret set for the session runtime. For the optional read-only S3 endpoint, see S3 client access.

packageR permits all browser origins (*) for public catalog access. To restrict origins, configure the Gateway to replace or remove backend CORS headers and handle preflight requests. Adding a header does not restrict the wildcard. Cookie-based cross-origin access needs a separate policy.

docs.title: EnvironmentConfig values and defaults
docs.text:
All paths below are relative to EnvironmentConfig.data. Defaults apply when a setting is omitted; example values such as cluster CIDRs, endpoints, and StorageClass names are not built-in defaults.

Select a specific EnvironmentConfig with the datalabs.pkg.internal/environment annotation or label to use its settings without per-Datalab overrides, as shown in the datalab-custom example. The annotation takes priority over the label; the default selection is datalab.

Runtime settings come from the EnvironmentConfig. The XRD retains unknown fields, but extra fields in spec do not override these settings.

docs.title: Runtime and service defaults
docs.text:
Setting Default Use defaults.vcluster.enabled true Virtual Kubernetes API for each started session. defaults.registry.enabled true Session Docker registry. defaults.registry.storage 5Gi Registry volume size. defaults.data.enabled true Shared packageR service and its configured endpoint. defaults.data.readOnlyMount false Read-only application permissions when enabled; storage IAM still applies. defaults.quota.memory 2Gi Session memory request. defaults.quota.storage 1Gi Workspace PVC size. defaults.quota.budget medium Session namespace budget. defaults.overallQuota.storage 100Gi Aggregate PVC request limit in the environment namespace. defaults.security.policy baseline Pod security level: restricted, baseline, or privileged. defaults.security.kubernetesAccess true Session Kubernetes service account token. defaults.security.kubernetesRole edit Session role: view, edit, or admin. defaults.security.externalEgress true Broad egress to the configured external CIDRs. defaults.persistence.storageClassName First allowed class, or cluster default Workspace StorageClass; a value outside the allowlist falls back to its first entry. defaults.files [] Workshop file bundles. packages [] Session extension packages.

File bundles and extension packages are passed to the session runtime unchanged. Set Data enablement before creating Datalabs because the runtime saves each environment's Workshop specification. See file sources for a file bundle example.

docs.title: Identity and endpoints
docs.text: Setting Default Use iam.realm default Keycloak realm; users must already exist here. iam.namespace keycloak Namespace selected by IAM egress rules. iam.issuerURL Not set Public login issuer; required for permanent Data exposure. iam.internalURL Not set Token and signing-key URL; required for permanent Data exposure. iam.extraAudiences [] Additional OAuth client audiences. ingress.enabled false Permanent Data Ingress; mutually exclusive with httpRoute.enabled. ingress.class Empty Session ingress class; required for Data Ingress. ingress.domain default for sessions Host suffix; must be set for permanent Data exposure. ingress.secret wildcard-tls for sessions TLS Secret; must be set for Data Ingress. ingress.annotations {} Annotations on the permanent Data Ingress. httpRoute.enabled false Permanent Data Gateway routes. httpRoute.enableS3 false Read-only S3 endpoint; requires httpRoute.enabled. httpRoute.parentName Not set Gateway name; required when Gateway exposure is enabled. httpRoute.parentNamespace Not set Gateway namespace; required when Gateway exposure is enabled. httpRoute.sectionName Not set HTTPS listener; required when Gateway exposure is enabled. httpRoute.httpSectionName Not set HTTP redirect listener; required when Gateway exposure is enabled.

docs.title: Storage and managed stores
docs.text:
Setting Default Use storage.endpoint Empty Endpoint reachable by runtime Pods; the input Secret's AWS_ENDPOINT_URL takes priority. storage.region Empty Object-store region; the input Secret's AWS_REGION takes priority. storage.type Empty rclone backend type, usually s3. storage.provider Empty for rclone; Other for the S3 proxy Object-store provider. storage.forcePathStyle true Path-style S3 requests. storage.secretNamespace Datalab namespace, or default Input storage Secret namespace. storageClasses.allowed [] Allowed workspace StorageClasses; an empty list permits any configured class. vcluster.storage 5Gi Default control-plane PVC size for named virtual clusters. vcluster.storageClasses.allowed Required when virtual clusters are declared Host classes exposed to virtual workloads. vcluster.storageClasses.default First allowed class Virtual workload default class. vcluster.storageClassName Virtual default class Control-plane StorageClass; must be allowed. vcluster.issuerCA System trust PEM CA for the HTTPS issuer. vcluster.discoveryURL Issuer discovery Optional HTTPS discovery address. vcluster.backendTLS.apiVersion gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1 BackendTLSPolicy API served by the Gateway. ingress.certificateAuthority System trust PEM Gateway CA embedded in profile kubeconfigs. database.storageClassName Cluster default PostgreSQL data StorageClass. database.backupStorageClassName Cluster default PostgreSQL backup StorageClass. database.tlsRoute.parentName Not set PostgreSQL Gateway name. database.tlsRoute.parentNamespace Not set PostgreSQL Gateway namespace. database.tlsRoute.sectionName Not set PostgreSQL TLS listener. documentStore.storageClassName Cluster default MongoDB data StorageClass. documentStore.backupStorageClassName Cluster default MongoDB backup StorageClass. cacheStore.storageClassName Cluster default Redis data StorageClass. cacheStore.backupStorageClassName Cluster default Redis backup StorageClass.

PostgreSQL TLSRoutes are created only when all three database.tlsRoute settings are present.

docs.title: Network rules
docs.text: Setting Default Use network.externalEgressCIDRs [] External destination ranges; empty means no broad external allow rule. network.blacklistIPs [] CIDRs excluded from external egress. network.podCIDRs [] Host Pod ranges excluded from external egress. network.serviceCIDR Not set Host Service range excluded from external egress. network.excludePolicies [] Generated policies to omit. network.internalEgress [] Explicit cross-namespace destinations. network.internalIngress [] Explicit cross-namespace sources. network.internalEgress[].namespace, network.internalIngress[].namespace Required for each entry Peer namespace. network.internalEgress[].podSelector, network.internalIngress[].podSelector {} Peer Pod selector; omitted means all Pods in the peer namespace. network.internalEgress[].ports, network.internalIngress[].ports [] Ports; omitted means all ports. network.internalEgress[].ports[].port, network.internalIngress[].ports[].port Required for each port entry Named or numbered port. network.internalEgress[].ports[].protocol, network.internalIngress[].ports[].protocol Kubernetes default (TCP) Port protocol. network.internalEgress[].ports[].endPort, network.internalIngress[].ports[].endPort Not set End of a numeric port range. network.internalIngress[].targetPodSelector {} Runtime Pods selected by the ingress policy; omitted means all runtime Pods.

docs.title: Network access
docs.text:
Set network.podCIDRs and network.serviceCIDR to the host cluster's network ranges. They are excluded from broad external egress so that it does not also allow access to other Datalab namespaces. Use the cluster configuration for the Service CIDR. A DNS Service IP alone does not identify the full range. Pod CIDRs can be listed with:

kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"  "}{.spec.podCIDR}{"  "}{.spec.podCIDRs}{"\n"}{end}'

Use 0.0.0.0/0 and ::/0 for all external IPv4 and IPv6 destinations, or list narrower ranges in network.externalEgressCIDRs.

For a backend Pod in another namespace, add an internalEgress entry:

network:
  internalEgress:
  - namespace: minio
    podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        v1.min.io/tenant: default
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 443
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 9000

Use network.internalIngress for inbound traffic. It uses the same fields as internalEgress, with namespace and podSelector selecting the source:

network:
  internalIngress:
  - namespace: operations
    podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: prometheus
    targetPodSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: package-r
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8888

These rules apply to existing runtime namespaces too. See Network policies for how policies combine, Data access, and policy exclusions.

docs.title: 5. Supply storage credentials
docs.text:
Create the object-storage bucket and credentials through your platform's storage process or Provider Storage. Provider Datalab reads an existing input Secret. Its name comes from spec.secretName, or the Datalab name when that field is omitted.

The Secret must exist in storage.secretNamespace and contain AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY. The storage identity must permit bucket listing with s3:ListAllMyBuckets. The endpoint must support path-style S3 requests.

For a manual setup, create the Secret with your credential values:

kubectl -n datalab create secret generic s-joe \
  --from-literal=AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID='<KEY_ID>' \
  --from-literal=AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY='<SECRET>'

Use the platform's Secret tools for shared installations. Keep live credentials out of Git.

docs.title: 6. Create a Datalab
docs.text:
Save this resource as datalab.yaml. The user joe must already exist in Keycloak. This uses the Joe example with an explicit claim namespace.

apiVersion: pkg.internal/v1beta2
kind: Datalab
metadata:
  name: s-joe
  namespace: workspace
spec:
  users:
  - joe

Apply it and check its conditions:

kubectl apply -f datalab.yaml
kubectl get datalabs -n workspace
kubectl describe datalab s-joe -n workspace

See Use a Datalab for session state, managed services, workshop files, and sharing.

docs.title: 7. Check the installation
docs.text:
Check that provider and function revisions are healthy and that the Datalab reports Synced=True and Ready=True:

kubectl get providers.pkg.crossplane.io
kubectl get providerrevisions.pkg.crossplane.io
kubectl get functions.pkg.crossplane.io
kubectl get functionrevisions.pkg.crossplane.io
kubectl get configurations.pkg.crossplane.io
kubectl get configurationrevisions.pkg.crossplane.io
kubectl get datalabs -n workspace

If reconciliation fails, read the Datalab conditions and events. Check that the required APIs are served. The provider APIs used here are namespaced:

kubectl api-resources --api-group=kubernetes.m.crossplane.io
kubectl api-resources --api-group=helm.m.crossplane.io
kubectl api-resources --api-group=keycloak.m.crossplane.io
kubectl api-resources --api-group=gateway.networking.k8s.io

For a managed store, also check its API group from the prerequisite table. Verify the Data address, storage access, and each requested service. If you declared a session, also check its browser login before giving users access.

docs.title: S3 client access
docs.text: The read-only S3 endpoint is experimental. Range reads currently return HTTP 200 with Content-Range, rather than HTTP 206.

docs.title: Enable the endpoint
docs.text:
Set httpRoute.enableS3: true in the selected EnvironmentConfig, with Gateway Data exposure configured as described under Data address. This adds the S3 endpoint to each Data-enabled Datalab's browser hostname.

Use a Gateway API controller that supports HTTPRoute header regular expressions, such as Contour. Add a ReferenceGrant if its certificate Secret is in another namespace. With S3 disabled, the routes serve only the browser. The network policies must permit access from the Gateway and access to object storage and IAM.

docs.title: S3 access to s-jane
docs.text:
The Jane example creates the Datalab s-jane and selects datalab-custom. With the example EnvironmentConfig, its endpoint is https://s-jane.lab.acme.com and its issuer is https://identity.acme.com/realms/acme. Replace these example DNS names with your environment's values.

Keycloak checks CLIENT_SECRET and issues a JWT. The AWS CLI sends it as AWS_SESSION_TOKEN in the X-Amz-Security-Token header. NGINX checks the tenant ID and passes the token to oauth2-proxy, which checks its signature, issuer, audience, expiry, and Datalab role. After authorization, rclone serve s3 checks the original AWS SigV4 request using s-jane as both signing values. It serves read-only data through separate upstream storage credentials.

AWS CLI
  │ HTTPS :443 → s-jane.lab.acme.com
  ▼
Contour / Envoy
  │ HTTP → Service data-s3 :8080
  ▼
NGINX gateway :8080
  ├─ Auth subrequest → oauth2-proxy 127.0.0.1:4180
  │                     └─ Fetch signing keys → Keycloak
  │                        (example internal URL: keycloak.keycloak:8080)
  │
  └─ If authorized → rclone 127.0.0.1:8081
                         └─ HTTPS → upstream S3 storage (s3.acme.com :443)

NGINX, oauth2-proxy, and rclone share the data-s3 Pod and use localhost for calls within that Pod. The Gateway implementation and upstream storage depend on your environment. The example internal Keycloak URL uses Service port 8080; other installations can use a different Service port.

Credential field Value AccessKeyId s-jane SecretAccessKey s-jane SessionToken Keycloak JWT access token Expiration Token expiry

The signing values are public tenant identifiers. They do not grant access without a valid JWT. The token must include s-jane in aud and at least one of ws_access, ws_admin, or ws_api under resource_access.s-jane.roles. These are Keycloak client roles, separate from OAuth scopes. All three permit reads. The upstream storage policy limits which buckets and objects the Datalab can read. Missing or invalid tokens cannot use a browser cookie or an unsigned request as a fallback.

The generated Datalab client adds its own audience when S3 is enabled. Other OAuth clients must emit the same audience and tenant roles. Service-account tokens do not need a verified email address.

The following Bash commands use the credential helper from the repository root. It uses the client credentials grant with s-jane as the client ID. At the prompt, enter the client_secret from the generated s-jane-oauth2-client Secret in the runtime namespace. The commands read bucket s-jane with path-style requests. Change the bucket name if your storage uses another name.

docs.title: Manual token retrieval
docs.text:
if [ -z "${CLIENT_SECRET:-}" ]; then
  CLIENT_SECRET="$(python3 -c 'import getpass; print(getpass.getpass("CLIENT_SECRET: "))')"
fi
export CLIENT_SECRET
export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=s-jane AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=s-jane
export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=https://s-jane.lab.acme.com
export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1
export AWS_PROFILE=s-jane
aws configure set s3.addressing_style path --profile s-jane

credentials="$(python3 tests/s3/s3-credentials.py \
  --tenant s-jane \
  --issuer https://identity.acme.com/realms/acme)"
AWS_SESSION_TOKEN="$(printf '%s' "$credentials" | \
  python3 -c 'import json, sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["SessionToken"])')"
export AWS_SESSION_TOKEN
unset credentials

aws s3 ls s3://s-jane/

Run the token retrieval command again after the token expires, or use automatic renewal below.

docs.title: Automatic token renewal with credential_process
docs.text:
Clear the manual AWS settings so that the CLI uses the profile's credential process. The CLI obtains new credentials when needed, using the helper's Expiration value.

unset AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY AWS_SESSION_TOKEN
unset AWS_CONFIG_FILE AWS_PROFILE AWS_ENDPOINT_URL
unset AWS_DEFAULT_REGION AWS_REGION

if [ -z "${CLIENT_SECRET:-}" ]; then
  CLIENT_SECRET="$(python3 -c 'import getpass; print(getpass.getpass("CLIENT_SECRET: "))')"
fi
export CLIENT_SECRET
export AWS_PROFILE=s-jane

aws configure set region us-east-1 --profile s-jane
aws configure set endpoint_url https://s-jane.lab.acme.com --profile s-jane
aws configure set s3.addressing_style path --profile s-jane
aws configure set credential_process \
  "python3 \"$PWD/tests/s3/s3-credentials.py\" --tenant s-jane --issuer https://identity.acme.com/realms/acme" \
  --profile s-jane

aws s3 ls s3://s-jane/

Keep CLIENT_SECRET available in the environment of the AWS CLI or SDK process. If you move the repository, update the helper's absolute path in the profile.

The endpoint supports list, HEAD, GET, and byte-range GET requests. It remains read only even when the Data browser has write permissions. Writes and presigned S3 URLs are rejected. packageR download and share links use the browser route.

docs.title: Use a Datalab
docs.text: A Datalab resource defines the users, sessions, and services for a team. The operator supplies the shared storage, identity, and network settings. Complete installation before applying these examples.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
A session is a named workspace with an editor, terminal, and persistent home directory. Declare the sessions you need in spec.sessions:

spec:
  sessions:
  - name: default
  - name: analysis
    state: stopped

The state defaults to started. A started session has a workspace Pod. A stopped session keeps its PVC without a running workspace. Change its state to started to use the same PVC again. Several sessions can run at once; each has its own Pod and PVC and shares the Datalab's credentials and managed services.

With no declared sessions, the Datalab still creates its shared services. It creates no session Pods or workspace PVCs.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text: Each declared session has a PVC mounted at /home/eduk8s. Its size and StorageClass come from the selected EnvironmentConfig. Use this volume for code, libraries, and workspace files. Keep datasets in object storage and database records in a managed database. Arrange backup and recovery with the operator.

docs.title: Managed service types
docs.text:
Each service field accepts one type. The API sets that type when you omit it. The API name for MongoDB is mongo.

Field Default type spec.databases postgres spec.documentStores mongo spec.cacheStores redis

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
Use spec.databases to request a PostgreSQL cluster and its logical databases:

spec:
  databases:
    pg0:
      names:
      - dev
      - prod
      storage: 1Gi
      backupStorage: 3Gi

This creates the pg0 cluster with dev and prod databases. The PostgreSQL operator manages the database Pods, credentials, and configured backups. Stopping a session does not stop the database.

Sessions receive connection settings such as POSTGRES_PG0_HOST, POSTGRES_PG0_PORT, and POSTGRES_PG0_DEV_URL. The generated <datalab>-datalab Secret holds these values. When the platform enables an external TLSRoute, it also supplies POSTGRES_PG0_DEV_URL_EXTERNAL. External connections require a client that supports direct TLS with SNI.

docs.title: Document and cache stores
docs.text:
Use these fields to request MongoDB and Redis stores:

spec:
  documentStores:
    prod:
      storage: 1Gi
      backupStorage: 3Gi
  cacheStores:
    prod:
      storage: 1Gi
      backupStorage: 3Gi

Each store needs its operator installed in the cluster. For the name prod, sessions receive MONGO_PROD_URI and REDIS_PROD_URL, along with separate host and credential fields where available.

The composition creates <store>-mongodb-auth and <store>-redis-auth Secrets. It watches their values and copies connection settings into <datalab>-datalab. Sessions import those settings as environment variables. Restart a session to load changed values.

docs.title: Backups
docs.text:
Set backupStorage to a positive Kubernetes storage quantity, such as 10Gi, to create a separate backup PVC. Zero or an omitted value disables backups without stopping the store.

Store Backup schedule Retention PostgreSQL pgBackRest: full on Sunday, differential on other days, at 01:00 in the operator's time zone. Four full backups and their dependent backups; the volume also holds WAL. MongoDB Full mongodump --oplog --gzip archive daily at 01:00 UTC. Four completed archives. Redis Full redis-cli --rdb snapshot daily at 01:00 UTC, checked with redis-check-rdb. Four completed snapshots.

Size the volume for retained backups and the next full export. Monitor failed Jobs and free space. Failed MongoDB or Redis jobs preserve completed backups. Enabling or disabling Redis backups restarts its Pod.

docs.title: Data and sharing
docs.text:
The Data service, packageR, is a file browser for the Datalab's object storage. A session's Data tab opens this shared service. With a permanent Data address, you can also use it without a running session.

The file browser requires sign-in. Share individual files through temporary download URLs, or folders through public share links. Recipients do not need a Datalab account.

The operator controls service availability and read-only permissions through EnvironmentConfig. Storage IAM limits every request. For read-only access with AWS tools, see S3 client access.

docs.title: Sharing data with the world
docs.text:
Put files in <datalab>/public in the bucket named after your Datalab, then send the public share link. For example, s-jane/public/results.csv belongs to the default public share for s-jane. A folder named public elsewhere is not shared automatically.

Public sharing needs a permanent Data address. Upload files through the Data browser when write access is allowed, or use your storage tools. Anyone with the link can browse and download those files without signing in.

docs.title: Files and the Workshop tab
docs.text:
The operator sets EnvironmentConfig.data.defaults.files to load workshop content from Git, an OCI image, or an HTTP archive. For example:

data:
  defaults:
    files:
    - git:
        url: https://github.com/versioneer-tech/datalab-example
        ref: origin/main
      includePaths:
      - /workshop/**
      path: .

Adding a source enables the Workshop tab. With no sources, the tab is hidden. Use includePaths, excludePaths, newRootPath, and path to select and place the files.

docs.title: Storage Secret
docs.text: Set spec.secretName to the input object-storage Secret name. If omitted, the Datalab name is used. The operator supplies the Secret and configures its namespace and endpoint during installation.

docs.title: Environment settings
docs.text: The selected EnvironmentConfig controls quotas, persistence, security, vCluster, registry, Data, and workshop content. See values and defaults for all settings, Session access for Kubernetes permissions, and Network policies for allowed traffic.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The named users must exist in Keycloak and their storage Secrets must exist before you apply these manifests in your claim namespace.

Manifest Environment Use Joe datalab Data without a session. Jeff, Jim, and Jane datalab Shared PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Redis stores; Jim has the Datalab admin role. Jane datalab-custom A started session and PostgreSQL. John datalab-custom Started and stopped sessions with workshop files.

The environment examples show the two configurations. datalab-custom demonstrates read-only Data, custom quotas and StorageClasses, privileged security with the Kubernetes admin role, vCluster, registry, file bundles, Gateway and S3 access, and internal network rules. Adapt these settings to your platform's access policy.

docs.title: Check provisioning
docs.text:
Check the Datalab conditions after applying a resource:

kubectl get datalabs -n workspace
kubectl describe datalab s-jeff -n workspace

Synced=True means the composition reconciled. Ready=True means its resources report ready. Read the conditions and events if either is false. Session state, phase, messages, and URLs remain in status.sessions. Virtual cluster access profiles are reported in status.connections. See API access for endpoints and Secret references.

docs.title: Connect to databases
docs.text:
Use the connection variables supplied to the session, such as POSTGRES_PG0_DEV_URL. The PostgreSQL operator also creates user Secrets named *-pguser-*. Use the database role assigned to your task; the postgres role has administrative access.

See Additional services for a psql example.

docs.title: Use a Datalab virtual cluster
docs.text:
Declare each virtual Kubernetes cluster under spec.vclusters:

apiVersion: pkg.internal/v1beta2
kind: Datalab
metadata:
  name: s-joe
  namespace: workspace
spec:
  users: [joe]
  vclusters:
    vc0:
      storage: 5Gi
      groups:
      - name: namespace-demo
        namespace: demo
        role: edit
      - name: cluster-admin
        namespace: "*"
        role: cluster-admin

Each entry creates one runtime in the Datalab namespace. Add vc1 alongside vc0 to create another cluster. An empty map creates none. Sessions and their environment-controlled vclusters remain separate.

docs.title: Platform settings
docs.text:
Merge these values into the Datalab's EnvironmentConfig:

data:
  iam:
    issuerURL: https://identity.example.org/realms/datalab
  ingress:
    domain: lab.acme.com
  httpRoute:
    enabled: true
    parentName: datalab
    parentNamespace: gateway-system
    sectionName: https
  vcluster:
    storage: 5Gi
    storageClasses:
      allowed: [standard]
      default: standard

The vcluster EnvironmentConfig section supplies defaults for all declared instances. spec.vclusters.<name>.storage overrides the control-plane PVC size. vcluster.storageClassName selects its class; otherwise the default class is used. Only classes in vcluster.storageClasses.allowed are exposed to virtual workloads. A host admission policy enforces this list for each syncer. Control-plane, workload, database, and session PVCs share the existing defaults.overallQuota.storage limit.

Apply dependencies/rbac.yaml. The host must serve ValidatingAdmissionPolicy and ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding. The Gateway must support HTTPRoute prefix rewriting, BackendTLSPolicy, and Kubernetes streaming requests. vcluster.backendTLS.apiVersion defaults to gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1; set it to the version served by your platform.

Set network.serviceCIDR and network.podCIDRs to the host ranges. Virtual workloads follow the environment's network policy. Managed databases in the same runtime namespace are reachable through their generated connection endpoints. Cross-namespace backends need an approved network.internalEgress rule. Virtual clusters share the host namespace and node kernel; their RBAC boundaries apply to their virtual APIs.

docs.title: API access
docs.text:
The generated kubeconfig for vc0 uses:

https://s-joe.lab.acme.com/.vc0

The Gateway removes /.vc0 and forwards to that instance. A separate backend TLS policy verifies its certificate. Each instance has its own selectors, credentials, provider configuration, and storage. Workload Ingress and Gateway synchronization is disabled. Use Kubernetes port forwarding to access a workload Service.

Each group creates a profile Secret in the Datalab claim namespace. Its name starts with <datalab>-vcluster-<instance>-<group>. Generated names have a stable hash suffix when a component has a hyphen or the full name needs shortening. status.connections reports the instance, group, endpoint, readiness, and Secret reference. It contains no credentials.

The Secret contains kubeconfig, client-id, client-secret, and issuer-url. The kubeconfig uses Python 3 to obtain short-lived tokens. Export the required profile and protect the file as a credential:

umask 077
profile_secret="$(kubectl -n workspace get datalab s-joe -o json | \
  jq -r '.status.connections[] | select(.instance == "vc0" and .group == "namespace-demo") | .secretRef.name')"
kubectl -n workspace get secret "${profile_secret}" \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.kubeconfig}' | base64 --decode > s-joe-vc0.kubeconfig
kubectl --kubeconfig ./s-joe-vc0.kubeconfig -n demo get pods

Roles are specific to an instance. A vc0 profile does not authorize vc1. Workspace roles alone do not authorize either virtual API. Namespace profiles can use view, edit, or admin. Use namespace: "*" with cluster-admin for virtual administration. The provider keeps the recovery kubeconfig private.

For a private issuer CA, set vcluster.issuerCA. An optional HTTPS vcluster.discoveryURL can provide separate discovery routing with the same issuer. For a private Gateway CA, set ingress.certificateAuthority.

docs.title: Datalab STAC catalog
docs.text:
The STAC workload example runs stac-fastapi-pgstac in virtual namespace demo. Its PostgreSQL database is a Datalab-managed service on the host. Add this request alongside vclusters:

databases:
  pg0:
    type: postgres
    names: [catalog]
    storage: 5Gi

PgSTAC requires PostGIS and a schema migration. The example migration Job uses the generated PostgreSQL credentials from the Datalab Secret. It creates a separate catalog login with the pgstac_ingest role. The API uses that login and the standard PostgreSQL settings: PGHOST, PGPORT, PGUSER, PGPASSWORD, and PGDATABASE.

PostgreSQL needs DNS and access to the host Kubernetes API for its controller. In a namespace with denied egress, approve these targets for the PostgreSQL Pods. Namespace selectors do not match host-network API endpoints on all CNIs. The integration has a PostgreSQL-specific policy for this case.

The example expects catalog-postgres-admin and catalog-postgres Secrets in virtual namespace demo. The first contains migration credentials. The second contains the API login. Supply these through your Secret process. Build the image from tests/vcluster/catalog.Dockerfile, push it to your registry, and replace __CATALOG_IMAGE__ with that image reference before applying the example. Wait for catalog-migrate to complete before starting the API Deployment. Remove the migration Secret after it completes.

Connect to the catalog through the generated profile:

kubectl --kubeconfig ./s-joe-vc0.kubeconfig -n demo \
  port-forward service/catalog 8080:8080

The catalog is available at http://localhost:8080. The example enables STAC transactions so a client can add collections and items. Its catalog records remain in PostgreSQL when the API Pod restarts.

Run tests/integration/run.bash verify-vcluster to check both virtual clusters, profile boundaries, persistent volumes, and the catalog. The catalog test creates a collection and item, searches it, restarts the API, and repeats the search after a control-plane restart.

docs.title: Removal
docs.text: Removing a group revokes its identity and binding while retaining its virtual namespace data. Removing an instance removes its runtime and control-plane PVC. Other instances, databases, sessions, and the shared namespace remain. Deletion follows the host StorageClass retention policy. Back up control-plane and database volumes before removing an instance or Datalab.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
Packages:

  • pkg.internal/v1beta2

docs.title: pkg.internal/v1beta2
docs.text:
Resource Types:

  • Datalab

docs.title: Datalab
docs.text:

A Datalab is a tenant-facing, namespaced composite resource. It defines membership, sessions, and data services.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
A session can use the credentials, volumes, Kubernetes permissions, and network access available to its Pod. The platform operator decides who may use them and sets the EnvironmentConfig.

Provider Datalab configures sessions and creates network policies. The cluster must enforce these controls through its CNI, admission rules, Pod security, and RBAC.

Control Details Browser sign-in, Datalab roles, and machine tokens Authentication Pod credentials, Kubernetes access, and privileged workloads Session access Allowed traffic and generated NetworkPolicies Network policies Files that readers can open without sign-in Public sharing

The platform team also manages node access, DNS, storage classes, quotas, cloud IAM, backup, retention, and audit. Check these controls together before giving users access to a Datalab.

docs.title: Network policies
docs.text: Provider Datalab creates egress and Data policies in the Datalab namespace. The cluster CNI must enforce Kubernetes NetworkPolicy for these rules to take effect.

docs.title: Generated egress policies
docs.text:
Policy Created when Allows deny-egress By default No egress by itself; other policies can allow traffic. allow-namespace-egress By default Traffic to Pods in the same runtime namespace. allow-dns-egress External egress, Data, or vCluster is enabled DNS to kube-system on TCP and UDP port 53. allow-vcluster-egress vCluster is enabled TCP ports 443 and 8443 to the same Datalab's vCluster control-plane Pods. allow-external-egress External egress is enabled The configured external CIDRs, minus excluded ranges. allow-internal-egress Internal targets are configured The selected backend Pods and ports in other namespaces.

The DNS rule lets Data resolve storage hosts and lets sessions resolve their vCluster Service. Namespace and Pod selectors on the vCluster rule limit it to the same Datalab.

NetworkPolicies are additive. deny-egress selects Pods for egress isolation; it does not override an allow rule in another selected policy. Check all policies that select a Pod when testing access.

docs.title: External and internal ranges
docs.text:
Supply the host Pod and Service CIDRs so that broad external egress does not also grant access to other Datalab namespaces. The rule excludes these ranges and the configured blacklist. Use explicit internal rules for required backends in other namespaces. See Network access for setup examples and the network reference for all fields.

With external egress disabled, same-namespace traffic, DNS needed by Data or vCluster, and access to the Datalab's vCluster API remain allowed. Standard NetworkPolicy cannot express ordered deny rules or DNS-name rules.

docs.title: Data service policies
docs.text:
For session access, packageR accepts port 8888 from session Pods. For permanent access, its OAuth proxy accepts port 4180. See Data and sharing for browser access and public links.

The S3 service accepts Gateway traffic on port 8080. Data and S3 proxies can reach IAM on TCP port 8080 in the configured IAM namespace. Object-storage access follows the Datalab's egress rules. Set iam.namespace to the namespace that contains the Keycloak Pods.

docs.title: Replace or exclude policies
docs.text:
Use EnvironmentConfig.data.network.excludePolicies only when another policy system provides the required controls. Excluding allow-dns-egress also suppresses the Data DNS policy.

Use RBAC and admission rules to limit who can change NetworkPolicies or select privileged and admin settings.

docs.title: Session access
docs.text: A Datalab session runs as a Pod in the host cluster. It can use its storage and service credentials, workspace PVC, and any other mounted volumes. Check these permissions together when deciding which code a user may run.

docs.title: Kubernetes and container access
docs.text:
The operator controls token availability and the Kubernetes role through defaults.security in the selected EnvironmentConfig. A session with vCluster enabled gets a virtual Kubernetes API. Its workloads still run on host Pods under the host's security and network rules. Without vCluster, the session uses its host namespace directly.

The privileged security policy enables Docker. Host mounts, runtime sockets, broad roles, and privileged containers can give session code access beyond its namespace. Give this access only to workloads that need it. See the configuration reference for the settings and defaults.

docs.title: Explain access to users
docs.text:
Tell users which data and services a session can use, whether Kubernetes and internet access are available, and whether Docker or privileged workloads are allowed. Explain what survives a stop or deletion, what is backed up, and who can restore it.

Stopping a Pod or tightening a network rule does not revoke a leaked credential. Rotate or revoke it at its source. Protect the generated OAuth Secret as described in Authentication.
